RO003-047----:
On a gentle SW-facing slope, c. 200m from the shore if an E arm of Lough Key, c. 800m NW of where the Boyle river leaves the lake. Two stones placed 7m apart are aligned WNW-ESE. The W stone (dims 1.65m x 0.25-0.5m; H 1.25m) is oriented NW-SE and the E stone (dims 1.95m x 0.2m; H 1.1m) is oriented NW-SE. (deValera and O'Nuallain 1972, 41)

RO003-062002-:
On a low rise in a low-lying landscape. An upright limestone stone (dims. 0.8m x 0.1m; H 0.75m) is inside the perimeter of rath (RO003-062001-) at ENE.

Date of upload: 24 August 2010
RO003-087----:
At the edge of a low bluff overlooking a slight NW-SE valley immediately to the N. The backstone (dims 1.55m x 0.2-0.35m; H 1.05m) of an E-W gallery (L c. 7m) survives in a clump of scrub together with some stones from the S side of a court (diam. c. 4m) at its E end.

Date of upload: 24 August 2010
RO004-009----:
On a shelf towards the bottom of the NE-facing slope of a drumlin. The remains of a segmented gallery (dims 4m NW-SE; 2.5m NE-SW) of which the two jamb stones and some sidestones on the SW side survive of the outer chamber. A jamb stone leading to a second chamber to the NW and one sidestone on the SW side of this chamber also survive. These are situated within a rectangular grass-covered stony mound (dims 17m NW-SE; 8m-10m NE-SW; H 0.5m). (deValera and O'Nuallain 1972, 31)

Date of upload: 24 August 2010

RO004-028----:
On limestone outcrop on a gentle S-facing slope. A segmented gallery of two chambers is aligned N-S. The N chamber (dims 2.8m NNE-SSW; c. 1.5m WNW-ESE) has only its W side complete while the S chamber (dims 3.05m NNE-SSW; 1.6m WNW-ESE) is almost complete. A subsidiary chamber (dims 1.8m N-S; 1.5m E-W) is just 3m W of the S chamber, while the N chamber opens into the remains of a court. The remains are surrounded by a grass-covered cairn (dims 16m N-S; 10-13m E-W; H 0.3-0.8m). (de Valera and O'Nuallain 1972, 31-2)
Compiled by: Michael Moore
Date of upload: 24 August 2010

RO004-029001-:
On a low rise in a flat low-lying landscape. An upright limestone slab (dims 1m N-S; 0.2m E-W; H 1.3m) rises through a rectangular grass-covered cairn (RO004-029002-) (dims 7.5m N-S; 7m E-W; H 0.1-0.5m) which has some whitethorn trees.
Compiled by: Michael Moore
Date of upload: 24 August 2010
RO004-062----:
At the crest of a N-facing slope in a clearing in mixed woodland overlooking Lough Meelagh, which is c. 120m to the N. This is a two-chambered gallery (L 8.2m NW-SE; Wth 1.15-1.6m NE-SW), of which the NW chamber survives complete with jamb stones, but the other chamber that was attached to a circular court (diam. 4.7-4.8m) is largely missing. Eight orthostats of the court remain upright, including the jamb-stones of the entrance to the gallary, and the court was probably open at SE. No lintels and no evidence of a cairn survive.
See the attached view taken from the SE.
See attached document with plan and sections of the monument.

Date of upload: 24 August 2010
RO004-063----:
Towards the top of the SW-facing slope of Kilronan Mountain in a clearing in a coniferous forest. Wedge-shaped chamber (int. dims 4.8m ENE-WSW; 1.8m NNW-SSE at E to 1.95m NNW-SSW at W) consisting of ten orthostats and a backstone (dims. 1.7m x 0.35m; H 0.75m) had a portico (dims 2m NNW-SSE; 1.35m ENE-WSW) at the W end separated from the chamber by a sillstone (dims 0.7m x 0.25m; H 0.3m) which does not block the opening. The stones are generally 0.3-0.6m high, and there are possible kerbstones of the original cairn to the SW of the gallery. No evidence of roofstones survives.
Compiled by: Michael Moore
Date of upload: 24 August 2010

RO005-015----:
Situated at the W end of a low E-W rise, c. 200m N of what was the E end of Lower Lough Gara which is now reclaimed. Rectangular chamber (int. dims.2.2m NW-SE; 1.95m NE-SW) facing NE defined by two sidestones and a backstone with two portal stones (H 1.75m; 2.2m) and the septal stone (H 1.9m). The roofstone (dims. 4m NE-SW; 3m NW-SE; T c. 0.7m) is in situ, and a slight grass-covered cairn (dims. c. 7m NW-SE; c. 6m NE-SW) surrounds the stones. Standing stone (RO005-016----) is c. 100m to the S. (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1972, 32,33)
It has been known and described from the early 19th century (Weld 1832, 278; D'Alton 1845, 81-2; Borlase 1897, vol. 1, 195-7; Clarke 1899, Ó Nualláin 1983, 100) and was excavated and conserved in 1954 (Topp 1962) when cremated human remains, a polished stone axe, two Bann flakes and a chert core were recovered (Herity 1964, 130).
See the attached view from the E

Date of upload: 24 August 2010

RO005-016----:
On a gentle S-facing slope c. 110m NE of the eastern end of Lower Lough Gara, which is now reclaimed, and the Boyle River. Sandstone block (dims. 1.1m x 0.55m; L 1.9m) which once stood c. 100m S of the portal tomb (RO005-015----), but was removed c. 1965 and now lies against a field bank.

RO006-118001-:
On top of the SW summit of a NE-SW ridge. Subcircular grass-covered area (dims 80m E-W; 73m N-S) defined by an earthen bank (Wth 7m at W to 11.3m at E; int. H 0.6m at W to 1.75m at E; ext. H 1.25-1.75m). There is no visible entrance and there is no surface evidence of the internal fosse and central platform recorded by Knox (1914b, 348). The large bowl-barrow (RO006-118002-) is outside the perimeter at E, and the perimeter of the enclose is straightened on this side. Bowl-barrow (RO010-001----) is c. 380m to the SW, and the henge (RO006-118007-) is c. 300m to the E. (Stout 1991, 283, west; Condit 1993)

RO006-118007-:
On a shelf of the SE-facing slope of a NE-SW ridge. Circular grass-covered area (diam. 63m N-S; 60m E-W) defined by an earthen bank (Wth 8-11.3m; int. H1.3-1.55m; ext. H 0.7-1.8m) S-W and a scarp down to the interior (H 0.55-1.35m) elsewhere. There is an entrance (Wth 6-6.5m) at SE, and the site is now on a golf-course. It is visible as a complete enclosure on aerial photographs (CUCAP: AHN 8; AJO 20; AVI 29,30) with a second entrance at N. A henge  (RO006-118001-) is c. 300m to the W, and barrows (RO006-118005-; RO006-118006-; RO006-118008-) are within 120-190m to the NNW, N and E. (Stout 1991, 283 east; Condit 1993,15)
Compiled by: Michael Moore
Date of upload: 24 August 2010
RO006-171----:
On a flat low-lying landscape within a golf-course. Described (de Valera and O 'Nuallain 1972, 33-4) as a gallery (dims 8.5m E-W; 1-1.7m N-S) with seven side-stones on the N and ten on the S sides, and with one lintel at the E end. The W end is separated by a septal stone from a portico (dims 1.5m x c. 1.5m) which has two facade stones to the N. It was within a trapezoidal cairn or mound (dims c. 10m E-W; c. 2.5m N-S at E to c. 7.5m N-S at W) defined by kerbstones at N and S. It is now visible as a circular, rounded and grass-covered mound (diam. c. 24m; H 1.6-2m) with the capstone of the gallery just visible on its summit. Rath (RO006-172----) is c. 80m to the SW.
Compiled by: Michael Moore
Date of upload: 24 August 2010

RO006-217----:
Located in deciduous woodland on a slight NW-facing slope towards the NW edge of a small E-W peninsula at the SE edge of Lough Key. It is also just N of a path associated with Cloontykilla Castle, a nineteenth century house, c. 130m to the SE. This is an upright sandstone (dims of base 0.66m x 0.22-0.41m; H 1.81m) aligned ENE-WSW and has a rounded top. It was first reported and recorded by Sam Moore.

RO007-024----:
Towards the bottom of the N-facing slope of a low E-W ridge. There is a single stone at NW (dims 1m x 0.3m; H 0.63m) and SE (dims 1.6m x 0.25m; H 0.25m). It may be a court tomb. Rath (RO007-025001-) is c. 140m to the SSW and enclosure (RO007-026----) is c. 140m to the SSE. (de Valera and O'Nuallain 1972, 34-5)

RO008C032----:

RO010-011----:
On a rise on a gentle S-facing slope. Described as an upright stone (dims c. 0.75m x c. 0.3m; H c. 3m) known as 'Clogh-na-Stuakeen' or the stone of the little hill and as 'Clogh-Cam' or the crooked stone (D'Alton 1845, 86), but D'Alton was confusing the latter name with that of a stone at Knocknacorha (RO010-049----) c. 4.5km  to the E. The stone at Tullyboy is no longer visible. Moylurg castle (RO010-010001-) is c. 140m to the W. Archaeological testing (06E1051) NW of the monument during 2006 produced no related material (Morahan 2010).
Compiled by: Michael Moore
Date of revised upload: 5 June 2015
RO010-049----:
Situated in a hollow at the bottom of the NW-facing slope of an ENE-WSW drumlin ridge. Marked on the 1837 and 1914 editions of the OS 6-inch map and described in gothic lettering on both as Cloghcrom - the crooked or leaning stone - and it was recorded thus by John O'Donovan in 1837 (O'Flanagan 1931, vol. 1, 120). It is a limestone slab (dims 0.7m x 0.45m; H 3m) oriented NE-SW and leaning to the NW, Rath (RO010-050----) is c. 100m to the SW.
During a battle which was fought in 1330 between Turlough O'Conor and Water Mac William Burke the latter was forced to retreat to Cairthe Liaghfada (ALC vol. 1, 613), which is identified as this stone (Connellan 1963), and it is known locally as An Lia Fada (Keenehan 2006 a). (Siggins 1986a)
Compiled by: Michael Moore
Date of upload: 24 August 2010
RO010-087001-:

Compiled by: Michael Moore
Date of upload: 24 August 2010
RO012-017----:

RO015-042001-:
On a gentle SW-facing slope. Trapezoidal overgrown cairn (dims 17m E-W; 6m N-S at W to c. 14m N-S at E) with some kerbstones at S and visible in an NE-SW field wall at N. The full court (dims 9m N-S; c. 8m E-W) at its E end consists of 7 stones on the S side and four surviving on the N. Two jambstones 0.6m apart allow access to the gallery (dims c. 5m E-W; 2.15m N-S), of which only one stone on the N side and two on the S side remain. There is a local tradition of its use as a children's burial ground (RO015-042002-).

RO022-057047-:
At the S edge of the Rathcroghan plateau, and on the summit of the mound of ring-barrow (RO022-057046-). Traditionally it was thought to mark the burial place of Daithaí, nephew of Niall of the Nine Hostages and the last of the early mythological High Kings of Ireland (O'Flanagan 1931, vol. 1, 85; Gormley 1989, 9, 10). The stone is known as An Coirthe Dearg – the red pillar stone (Kavanagh 2013, 109). The stone fell in the mid-19th century and was re-erected, and its base was investigated in 1913. It is a siltstone upright (dims 1.35m x 0.25m; max. H 1.83m) aligned N-S and with a crest sloping down to the N. (Knox, 1914a, 35-6; Herity 1983, 132; 1984, 134; Waddell 1983, 29-31; 1987-8; 1988, 10-12)
This is a National Monument in state ownership: No. 473

RO032-001001-:
At the summit of Kiltullagh Hill with a modern quarry c. 30m to the S in Co. Mayo where human remains dating to 3rd to 6th century AD were found in 1991 (Cribin et al. 1994). This is a rectangular stone (dims 0.7m x 0.2m; H 1.2m) aligned ENE-WSW with three holes (dims 0.04-0.06m; D 0.04-0.05m) in its W edge. Excavation (94E0030) around its base (McCormick 1994) revealed a fourth hole on its W edge together with a male inhumation and pieces of a cremation burial (RO032-001004-). Further excavation (96E0179) recovered more inhumations and a cremation were found in the vicinity (Robinson and Coombs 2000, 179). Ring-barrow (RO032-001002-) is c. 5m to the NE, but a second ring-barrow (RO032-001003-) (Knox 1914a, 45-6, Ring No. 1), whose position is uncertain lay to the W, and is probably in Co. Mayo.
